flags: minor: B-D are weak; C and D have no textual support at all, so the item is mostly a matter of recognizing the controlled-comparison logic
R034-01.notes: The sentence, plus the follow-up listing that the match, investments and opt-out freedom were unchanged, isolates the default as the cause of the participation jump.

R034-02.notes: The context is that doing nothing is the norm, so whatever default is picked decides outcomes. A and C read a self-interest/bias meaning into 'neutral' (an attractive trap); D contradicts 'does not forbid anything'.

flags: minor: A 'trained' and B 'strengthened' are the physical-exercise trap meanings; the trap is standard and fair
R034-03.notes: Freedom is exercised (used) by busy, distracted people.

R034-04.notes: 'Less loudly' means it was less publicized than the participation finding ('No one disputes...'). 'Early studies also revealed' rules out A; nothing supports C or D.

R034-05.notes: 'Not a flaw in the idea so much as the idea itself, seen from the other side': the same inertia that makes defaults work also traps people. B conflicts with 'millions of accounts'; D conflicts with 'No one disputes'; C is off topic.

flags: minor: B is contradicted by the passage ('few later bothered to stop them' implies they could stop)
minor: overlaps somewhat with R034-07, since both items are about the same escalation program, but they test different features
R034-06.notes: The increases come from future raises rather than current pay, so take-home pay never drops. This is one inference from a single sentence.

R034-07.notes: Passage B says employees 'agreed in advance'; Passage A's rule enrolled people automatically, with no prior consent. A describes Passage A's own rule (the opt-out form), which is a good trap for readers who mix up the passages. B contradicts the passage's 'future pay'; D is unsupported.

flags: minor: Passage A never states outright that enrolled workers saved more; that impression is only implied ('accomplish what years of reminders and lectures about saving could not'). The key is defensible but rests on an implied impression, which matches the stem's wording 'impression'
minor: overlaps conceptually with R034-09 (both rest on the B sentence that some would-be savers ended up saving less)
R034-08.notes: Passage B shows people stuck at low default rates and some saving less, which complicates the idea that higher participation means more saving. A and B are facts that Passage B does not dispute ('No one disputes...'). C, about freedom, is a plausible distractor, but Passage B's point is about inertia rather than freedom, and the item asks specifically about contribution rates.

flags: minor: the key closely paraphrases one Passage B sentence ('Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less'), so for students who find that sentence the item becomes close to a lookup
minor: B and D are traps drawn from Passage A's finding that young and low-income workers benefited most; they are fair traps
R034-09.notes: Workers who would have saved more on their own were anchored at the low default. B and D describe workers who gained participation, and A describes workers who escaped the default.

passage_notes: Factual check: Passage A matches Madrian & Shea (2001). The firm switched to automatic enrollment in 1998; participation was about 37% under the old rule versus about 86% under the new one; the default was a 3% contribution into a money market fund; and the effects were largest for young and low-income workers. Passage B's escalation program matches Save More Tomorrow (Thaler & Benartzi 2004), in which savings rates went from about 3.5% to 13.6% over roughly 40 months. 'More than tripled' is accurate. No factual problems found.
